guide.title: Unit 2: Audience, evidence, and thesis: review guide
guide.intro: Writers choose evidence and build a thesis with a particular audience in mind. This unit practices reading those choices and making them yourself: matching evidence to what an audience values, and writing a thesis that is arguable and previews the argument.

sections.title: Audience and purpose
body: Writers adapt to what their audience already believes, values, and needs. A skeptical audience may need common ground before a request; an audience that agrees may need a reason to act now.

Ask: what does this audience care about most (money, safety, fairness, tradition, their children)? Which details seem chosen because of that? A writer who shares the audience's background may mention it to build credibility.
points: The same claim can be argued with different evidence for different audiences.
Notice what a writer assumes the audience already knows.

sections.title: Strategic evidence and structure
body: Strategic evidence is not just true; it is chosen because it will matter to this audience and supports this particular claim. Writers often order evidence to build a line of reasoning, for example from the problem, to its cause, to the solution.
When integrating evidence, introduce its source, keep the quotation or statistic short, and follow it with commentary that explains what it shows.
points: Introduce a source's authority before quoting it.
Place evidence next to the claim it supports.
Order body paragraphs so each builds on the last.

sections.title: Thesis statements
body: A thesis states the writer's position on an issue in a way that requires proof or defense. A fact (“The library opens at nine”) is not a thesis; a position (“The library should open at seven so commuters can use it”) is.
A thesis may preview the structure of the argument by naming its main reasons in the order they will appear.
points: Test a thesis by asking whether someone could reasonably disagree.
A preview lists reasons in the same order as the body paragraphs.
Avoid announcing (“In this essay I will…”); state the position.

example.prompt: Turn this topic into an arguable thesis that previews its reasons: “School lunch.”
example.solution: “Our school should lengthen lunch to forty minutes, because students currently skip meals to make it through the line, rushed eating hurts afternoon focus, and a longer break would cost no instructional time if passing periods were shortened.”

misconceptions: “A thesis is the topic of the essay.”
A thesis is the arguable position on the topic.
Evidence is strong when it fits the claim and matters to the audience.
“A writer should never mention their own background.”
Shared experience can build credibility with an audience.
Evidence needs an introduction and commentary to show what it proves.

passages.title: Passage 1: Remarks at a meeting of the Main Street Merchants Association
text: (1) I know what many of you are thinking, because I thought it too. When the city proposed replacing a row of parking spaces on Main Street with a protected bike lane, I wrote a letter against it. I have run this hardware store for nineteen years, and I believed every lost space was a lost customer.

(2) Then I drove to Fairview, where the same change was made three years ago, and I asked the shop owners there to show me their numbers. Of the eleven I spoke with, nine said their sales were the same or higher. The bakery owner showed me her receipts: weekday sales up eight percent.
(3) People on bikes, it turns out, stop more often. They don't need to circle for a space, and they can't carry a week's groceries, so they come back.
(4) I am not asking you to love bicycles. I am asking you to look at the receipts before we oppose something that may help our registers.

passages.title: Passage 2: A pediatric dentist on school vending machines
text: (1) Parents, we want the same thing: children who can sit through an afternoon class without a toothache. That is why I am asking our school board to replace sugary drinks in vending machines with water and milk. My reasons are cost, comfort, and habit.
(2) First, cost. A single filling can run well over a hundred dollars, and many families pay it out of pocket.
(3) Second, comfort. Last month an eight-year-old patient told me she hides her mouth when she laughs. She had four cavities, and she drinks two sodas a day, both bought at school.
(4) Third, habit. Children copy what is easy. If the easy choice at school is water, they will carry that habit home.

passages.title: Draft 1: An essay introduction about personal finance classes
text: The following is a draft introduction to a student's argument for the school board. It may need revision.

(1) Many graduates leave high school without knowing how to read a pay stub or a loan agreement. (2) Our district offers one personal finance elective, and it fills up in minutes. (3) Personal finance is a subject. (4) The board should make a one-semester personal finance course a graduation requirement.

passages.title: Draft 2: A student paragraph about free museum days
text: The following is a draft of a student's paragraph for a letter to the city council. It may need revision.

(1) The city museum should offer one free day each month. (2) Ticket prices have risen to eighteen dollars. (3) Families with several children may find that cost hard to justify. (4) The museum's director said, “Attendance on our last free day was triple a normal Saturday.” (5) A free day would bring in visitors who might later become members.

questions.prompt: Whom is the speaker mainly trying to persuade?
choices: City officials who designed and proposed the new bike lane
Fellow shop owners who fear the bike lane will hurt sales
Cyclists who want more bike lanes on Main Street
Shop owners in Fairview, where the change was made years ago
questions.explanation: He addresses the association's members and responds to their worry about lost parking and customers.
choiceExplanations: He mentions the city's proposal but speaks to fellow merchants.
He says he isn't asking anyone to love bicycles; cyclists aren't the audience.
Fairview's owners are his sources of evidence, not his listeners.

questions.prompt: Which best states the speaker's main claim?
choices: The city should not remove parking spaces from Main Street, because every space is a customer
Fairview's bakery has grown more successful since its bike lane opened
Bicycles are a better way than cars to travel to Main Street shops
Merchants should examine the evidence before opposing the bike lane, which may help sales
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 asks merchants to look at the receipts before opposing a change that may help them.
choiceExplanations: This was close to his earlier view, which he has changed.
The bakery is one piece of evidence, not the main claim.
He explicitly declines to argue that bicycles are better than cars.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker begin by saying he once opposed the bike lane himself?
choices: To apologize to the city for the letter he once wrote opposing its bike lane proposal
To build common ground and credibility with listeners who share his original concern
To show that he dislikes changing his mind once he has decided
To introduce statistics about how many people ride bicycles
questions.explanation: By sharing their fear and his long experience as a merchant, he makes his change of mind persuasive to a skeptical audience.
choiceExplanations: He doesn't apologize to anyone; he explains how evidence changed his view.
The point is that he did change his mind.
The statistics in paragraph 2 are about sales, not about riders.

questions.prompt: The speaker relies on sales figures from Fairview shop owners rather than, for example, data on how many people ride bikes. What does this choice suggest?
choices: He believes cycling statistics are always inaccurate
He chose evidence that speaks to his audience's main concern: revenue
He wants to change the audience's opinion of cyclists
He has no access to traffic data from the city or from the town of Fairview
questions.explanation: Merchants worry about sales, so evidence about other merchants' receipts addresses that concern directly.
choiceExplanations: He never comments on the accuracy of other statistics.
He explicitly says he isn't asking them to love bicycles.
Nothing in the passage suggests he lacked traffic data.

questions.prompt: Who is the intended audience of the passage?
choices: Companies that stock the vending machines
Other dentists in the community
The eight-year-old patient and her family
Parents of students at the school
questions.explanation: The writer opens with “Parents, we want the same thing.”
choiceExplanations: The companies that stock the machines are never addressed.
Other dentists aren't addressed.
The patient is an example in the argument, not its audience.

questions.prompt: In paragraph 1, the sentence “My reasons are cost, comfort, and habit” mainly serves to
choices: introduce a counterargument that the writer will rebut
state a fact that settles the argument at once
preview the structure of the argument that follows
describe the writer's credentials as a pediatric dentist
questions.explanation: The three reasons are then developed in order, in paragraphs 2, 3, and 4.
choiceExplanations: No opposing view is introduced or rebutted.
It previews reasons that are developed afterward; it settles nothing by itself.
The writer's role as a dentist is clear from the title, not from this sentence.

questions.prompt: The story of the eight-year-old patient in paragraph 3 primarily
choices: makes the reason “comfort” concrete with an example parents can picture
explains how much the patient's fillings cost her family
proves that every child who drinks soda at school will soon get several cavities
shows that the writer's patients are mostly young
questions.explanation: A specific child hiding her smile shows what “comfort” means emotionally and physically.
choiceExplanations: Cost is discussed in paragraph 2; the patient's story does not give her family's costs.
One example can't prove a universal claim, and the writer doesn't claim it does.
The writer doesn't describe her practice's patients overall.

questions.prompt: How does the opening sentence (“we want the same thing”) relate to the writer's purpose?
choices: It shifts the argument's focus from children's health to the work of dentists
It concedes that the request is unpopular with many parents
It frames the request as serving a goal parents already hold, so they will support it
It suggests that parents disagree with the school board about what vending machines should sell
questions.explanation: Starting from shared values lets the writer present the vending change as a way to reach the parents' own goal.
choiceExplanations: The focus stays on children's health.
The writer doesn't concede anything about how popular the request is.
The writer wants parents to support the board, not oppose it.

questions.prompt: Which sentence in the draft functions as the thesis?
choices: Sentence (1)
Sentence (4)
Sentence (3)
Sentence (2)
questions.explanation: Sentence (4) takes an arguable position: the course should be a graduation requirement.
choiceExplanations: Sentence (1) describes the problem.
Sentence (3) is a vague statement of fact.
Sentence (2) gives evidence of demand.

questions.prompt: The writer plans body paragraphs on (a) real-world mistakes graduates make, (b) the elective's waiting list, and (c) the low cost of the change. Which revision of sentence (4) best previews them in order?
choices: The board should require a personal finance course, because graduates make costly mistakes, students want the class, and it would cost little.
The board should require personal finance because it is an important subject that nearly any graduate will use throughout the rest of adult life.
Because the change would cost little, the board should consider personal finance.
Personal finance should be required for graduation, and in this essay I will explain the reasons why the board should agree.
questions.explanation: This version states the position and lists the three reasons in the order the essay will develop them.
choiceExplanations: It gives no specific reasons.
It previews only one reason, and out of order.
It announces the essay instead of previewing the specific reasons.

questions.prompt: Should the writer keep or delete sentence (3)?
choices: Delete it, because it states the obvious and adds no support
Keep it, because it is the thesis of the introduction
Keep it, because it gives a statistic about demand for the elective
Delete it, because it contradicts sentence (2)
questions.explanation: “Personal finance is a subject” neither makes a claim nor supports one.
choiceExplanations: Sentence (4) is the thesis of the introduction.
It contains no statistic about the elective or anything else.
It doesn't contradict anything.

questions.prompt: Board members are concerned about crowded schedules. Which sentence, added before sentence (4), would best address that concern?
choices: Board members should not worry about crowded schedules, because students can usually find room in their day for a class that matters this much.
Students already have too many required classes, and many have little room left for electives.
Some students prefer art classes.
The course could replace the computer applications requirement, which covers similar spreadsheet skills, so schedules would not grow.
questions.explanation: This answers the audience's specific concern with a practical solution, which makes the thesis easier to accept.
choiceExplanations: This dismisses the concern without a reason.
This strengthens the board's concern without answering it.
This is unrelated to the concern or the thesis.

questions.prompt: Which sentence provides the strongest evidence that a free day would increase attendance?
choices: Sentence (5)
Sentence (3)
Sentence (4)
Sentence (2)
questions.explanation: The director's report that a past free day tripled attendance is direct evidence.
choiceExplanations: Sentence (5) predicts a benefit without evidence.
Sentence (3) is a reason families might stay away.
Sentence (2) explains a cost, not what a free day would do.

questions.prompt: The writer wants to introduce the quotation in sentence (4) so that readers understand why it is credible. Which revision is best?
choices: Someone said, “Attendance on our last free day was triple a normal Saturday.”
“Attendance on our last free day was triple a normal Saturday,” which is a quotation from someone who works at the museum.
The museum's director said something about attendance.
Maria Ortiz, who has directed the museum for ten years and tracks its attendance, said, “Attendance on our last free day was triple a normal Saturday.”
questions.explanation: Naming the source and her relevant role tells readers why her numbers can be trusted.
choiceExplanations: “Someone” gives readers no reason to trust the claim.
Saying it comes from “someone at the museum” still gives readers no reason to trust it.
Paraphrasing vaguely loses the specific evidence.

questions.prompt: The letter is for the city council, which funds the museum. Which sentence, added after sentence (5), would best appeal to this audience?
choices: The writer's favorite exhibit is the dinosaur hall, which opened in the museum last year.
Many other cities have beautiful museums that attract tourists each year.
Membership fees and gift shop sales on free days could offset lost ticket revenue.
Museums are fun places to visit with family members of many ages.
questions.explanation: A council that funds the museum will care whether the plan affects the budget.
choiceExplanations: A personal preference doesn't address the council's concerns about funding.
Other cities' museums don't address this museum or its budget.
This is too general to persuade a funding body about cost.

questions.prompt: Which order of sentences (2) through (5) best reflects a clear line of reasoning from problem to evidence to benefit?
questions.explanation: The draft already moves from the cost problem, to who it affects, to evidence that a free day works, to the longer-term benefit.
choiceExplanations: This separates the cost from the families it affects.
This starts with the benefit and ends with the problem.
This puts the evidence before the problem it addresses.
